10.1002_adfm.79020: Second coordination shell (SCS) engineering offers a powerful strategy for fine‐tuning the intrinsic activity of Fe–N‐C single‐atom catalysts, yet achieving targeted SCS regulation remains a formidable synthetic challenge. Herein, we propose a rational precursor‐engineering approach driven by the steric hindrance of pyrazole‐borate ligands to precisely construct Fe─N 4 sites with tunable boron SCS doping levels. The optimized FeN 4 B 3 /NC catalyst exhibits an exceptional half‐wave potential of 0.92 V for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) in alkaline media and a specific energy density of 967.03 Wh kg Zn −1 in a zinc‐air battery. Combined experimental and theoretical investigations reveal that second‐shell boron coordination induces ligand‐field asymmetry around the Fe center, leading to an occupancy transition of ‐to‐ in the Fe 3 orbital. This reconfiguration of Fe 3d electron distribution fine‐tunes the adsorption energetics by forcing electron injection into the Fe─O σ∗ anti‐bonding orbital, which generates enhanced Pauli repulsion to weaken the * OH binding affinity and accelerate its desorption. This work demonstrates the pivotal role of the SCS environment in intrinsic activity modulation but also provides an orbital‐level design principle for high‐performance single‐atom catalysts.
10.1002_advs.77998: Direct seawater oxygen evolution reaction (OER) is critically hampered by chloride‐induced competitive oxidation, corrosion, and active‐site poisoning, driving the urgent need for highly active and chlorine‐tolerant electrocatalysts. Herein, a surface‐engineered electrocatalyst comprising osmium nanoparticles (Os NPs) anchored onto CoFe layered double hydroxide (Os/CoFe LDH) was prepared. X‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy revealed that the incorporated Os NPs stabilized high‐valence Co/Fe species, which preferentially promote OH − adsorption over Cl − and function as the genuine active centers for OER. Furthermore, in situ Raman spectroscopy demonstrates that Os NPs anchoring modulates the interfacial water structure, thereby enhancing water adsorption and facilitating seawater OER kinetics. The optimized Os/CoFe LDH‐40 achieves an overpotential of only 244 mV at 10 mA cm −2 in simulated alkaline seawater and operates stably for over 300 h in an anion exchange membrane electrolyzer at 300 mA cm −2 . This work not only develops a high‐performance catalyst for alkaline seawater OER but also offers new perspectives for advancing osmium‐based materials in electrocatalysis.
10.1016_j.ceramint.2026.07.416: This paper presents the study of the influence of B-site doping (Ni/Cu ratio in the B-site) and A-site deficiency on the microstructural, electrical and electrochemical properties of (La 0.25 Sr 0.25 Ca 0.45 ) y Ti 0.95 Ni 0.05-x Cu x O 3-δ (LSCTNC A- ) solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) anode material. Doping of La 0.25 Sr 0.25 Ca 0.45 TiO 3-δ (LSCT A- ) with Ni aiming to enhance the electrochemical performance of the anode materials and Cu is added as an interesting co-dopant. It has been demonstrated that the crystallographic parameters and electrical as well as electrochemical properties are influenced by the oxygen partial pressure, A-site deficiency, and the Ni/Cu ratio at the B-site. Doping with Cu modifies the lattice parameters, i.e the bond lengths and angles between atoms. Impedance spectroscopy shows that A-site deficiency and Ni/Cu ratio in the B-site affect significantly the mid-frequency ( R mid ) and low-frequency ( R low ) polarization resistances. Total polarization resistance is dominantly defined by R low . Doping with Cu improved material conductivity only in the case of 10% A-site deficiency. No enhancement in polarization resistance in H 2 /H 2 O system or stability was found when Ni was replaced with Cu.
10.1016_j.ijhydene.2026.154043: Fuel cell membrane deformation and durability can be affected by holes at the surface of the gas diffusion layers (GDLs). To improve quality control for fuel cell manufacturing, it is important to understand the severity level of the holes, so that subsequent mitigation measures can be taken. In this work, the impact of GDL holes on membrane deformation is investigated using X-ray computed tomography as the primary investigative tool combined with a computationally inexpensive finite element model that utilizes spring foundation to simulate the compressive load of the GDL. Based on consistent experimental and simulation results, the critical threshold GDL hole diameter that is capable of inducing membrane buckling related failure is 100 ± 10 μm under the flow channel, below which the influence of GDL holes on membrane deformation is insignificant. However, GDL holes of any size can cause membrane buckling under the land due to locally elevated through-plane compression. As a mitigation strategy, membrane buckling can be suppressed by reducing the membrane thickness. Thinner membranes can effectively reduce water uptake during relative humidity cycles, thus reducing membrane deformation induced by cyclic expansion and shrinkage. • Combined visualization and modeling analysis of membrane buckling deformation. • Under channels: a threshold hole dimension is required to trigger membrane buckling. • Under lands: any gas diffusion layer hole dimensions trigger membrane buckling. • A strong impact of in-plane friction on buckling onset and progression is revealed. • Thinner membranes shown to effectively reduce buckling and stress concentration.
10.1016_j.scs.2025.107003: • Assessment of flood disruptions on road networks using two quantitative approaches. • GIS analysis provides a preliminary vulnerability evaluation of road networks. • Mesoscopic simulation captures traffic dynamics and quantifies flood impacts. • Both methods estimate significant increases in travel times and distances. • Results confirm the effectiveness of combining GIS and traffic network analysis. Road networks serve as a critical lifeline for ensuring the mobility of people and goods. The increasing frequency and unpredictability of extreme weather events highlight the need for studies to identify potential vulnerabilities of road networks and assess the negative effects of disruptions on traffic flows. This paper investigates the vulnerability of road networks to flood-induced disruptions, emphasising the use of open data and open-source software tools. Two quantitative approaches are proposed and compared: (i) a GIS-based spatial and topological analysis that assesses network vulnerability without incorporating traffic demand, and (ii) mesoscopic traffic simulation with dynamic traffic assignment to evaluate network performance and functionality under disrupted conditions. These methodologies are applied to a case study in Northern Italy, highlighting their different levels of complexity and applicability depending on data availability. The results indicate that while the spatial and topological approach provides a preliminary identification of vulnerabilities, the simulation method offers a detailed understanding of the dynamic traffic flows under degraded conditions, capturing not only changes in travel distance and time but also the effects of congestion.
10.1021_acs.est.6c00957: Micropollutants represent growing risks to water quality and human health, necessitating solutions beyond conventional treatment. While ultraviolet-based advanced oxidation processes (UV-AOPs) effectively degrade those micropollutants, their implementation is complex because of difficulties in predicting treatment performance, deriving kinetic parameters, inferring reaction mechanisms, and optimizing energy-intensive operations. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) are providing novel, data-driven solutions to these long-standing challenges. This work provides an overview on the rapid progress in leveraging ML to model UV-AOPs, including forecasting micropollutant degradation efficacy, estimating bimolecular rate constants of radicals with micropollutants, mapping plausible transformation pathways of micropollutants in various UV-AOPs, and performing intelligent optimization toward operating parameters. We also discuss the challenges, research gaps, and future directions, involving embedding physicochemical principles into interpretable ML frameworks, integrating real-time control, advancing prediction of byproduct toxicity, and the development of LLM (large language model)-assisted knowledge infrastructure, ultimately enabling smarter, more efficient, and safer UV-AOP systems and fostering deeper integration of data science and water treatment engineering.
10.1039_d5ta08243a: Imidazole–carbonate inner-salt ionic liquids enhance ion transport via strong Li + coordination. Their frontier orbital energies stabilize SEI/CEI and suppress decomposition, enabling ME-10 to achieve high rate capability, stability, and capacity.
10.5194_hess-30-6207-2026: One of the most important skills of hydrological models is to simulate timing and magnitude of flood events. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks are currently among the most successful models for streamflow and flood prediction over large regions. In snow-influenced catchments, which typically comprise a minority in large-scale studies, floods are generated by two distinctly different processes, snowmelt and rainfall. The applicability of hydrological models in such regions is therefore dependent on their ability to represent both types of floods. Nevertheless, flood evaluations of LSTM taking different flood-generating processes into account are currently lacking. This study fills this gap by evaluating the ability of LSTM to model flood peak characteristics separately for snowmelt and rainfall generated floods. The trained LSTM model successfully simulated streamflow time series across the 103 evaluated catchments, with average NSE of 0.85 and average KGE of 0.87 over the unseen evaluation period. LSTM exhibited better performance in the majority of the catchments in terms of flood peak timing and magnitude for both rainfall and snowfall generated floods when compared to the operational hydrological model in the region (HBV) used as a benchmark. Both models had a 24 pp higher percentage of correctly simulated peak days for rainfall generated floods as compared to snowmelt generated floods. LSTM outperformed HBV for a larger proportion of the catchments in terms of peak timing of rainfall generated events (83 %) as compared to snowmelt generated events (64 %). On the other hand, a larger proportion of the catchments were improved by LSTM for snowmelt generated events as compared to rainfall generated events when considering peak magnitudes. The largest improvements in peak magnitudes were found for rainfall generated events, in particular for catchments where HBV exhibited high (> 40 %) absolute errors. Overall, our findings bring confidence that LSTM can improve hydrological services in regions subject to both snowmelt and rainfall generated floods.
